cent.-3000.moved: Copper and lapis move down the Euphrates and across the Gulf; writing has just begun in Sumer and Egypt.
cent.-3000.art: Cylinder seals and the Warka vase at Uruk; slate palettes and the first royal tombs at Abydos; painted pottery on the Indus and in the Yellow River villages.
cent.-3000.life: The Nile has one king. Narmer’s heirs rule from Memphis in the double crown, their scribes are learning hieroglyphs and their governors count the harvest, while almost everyone else farms from a house of mud brick, sowing when the flood goes down in October and reaping from March. On the lower Yangtze, Liangzhu walls in some three square kilometres, threaded by thirty kilometres of canals with eight water gates and guarded by dams in the hills; its lords go to the grave under heaps of jade.
cent.-3000.food: Emmer bread ground on saddle querns, gritty enough to wear down the teeth, barley beer every day, onions, garlic, lentils and fish by the Nile; rice from the silos of Liangzhu.
cent.-3000.smell: An Egyptian village smelled of river mud and drying brick, of emmer pounded and spread in the sun, and of beer bread crumbled into water to ferment.
cent.-3000.trouble: The first kingdom asks who owns the harvest and the labour: Egypt’s farmers owe the state work on its canals and buildings, and the realm Narmer joined by war in the Delta already reaches into Canaan and Nubia.
cent.-3000.powers.0.t: the First Dynasty, from about 3100 BC, rules the whole Nile valley
cent.-3000.powers.1.t: temple cities of the lower Euphrates; cuneiform in use
cent.-3000.powers.2.t: the Kot Diji phase, before the great cities
cent.-2900.moved: Grain and wool move by canal in Sumer; Egypt trades up the Nile for gold and ivory and by sea to Byblos for cedar.
cent.-2900.art: Mud-brick temples on platforms in Sumer; mastaba tombs and ivory carving in Egypt; stamp seals and fine wheel-made pottery on the Indus.
cent.-2900.life: Sumer is a land of about thirteen walled cities, each round its temple and ruled by a lugal or an ensi, its barley and date palms fed by canals. Uruk may hold 50,000 to 80,000 people, and in some districts three people in four live in town. At the north-western edge of the farming world, on Orkney, the families of Skara Brae sit round a central hearth in stone houses with box beds and a stone dresser facing the door, banked against the wind with their own midden.
cent.-2900.food: Barley bread and beer, dates, mutton and goat in Sumer; on Orkney, beef, pork and mutton, barley, fish and shellfish, stored in Grooved Ware jars that hold up to thirty litres.
cent.-2900.smell: Skara Brae smelled of hearth smoke trapped under the roofs and of fish bones and shells in the midden packed round its walls; a Sumerian city of canal water and of sheep and goats brought in from the pastures.
cent.-2900.trouble: Water and boundaries: the cities of Sumer, divided by canals and boundary stones, quarrel over irrigated land, as Lagash and Umma will for generations.
cent.-2900.powers.1.t: Ur, Uruk, Kish and Lagash contend
cent.-2900.powers.2.t: walled towns on the Ravi and Indus
cent.-2800.moved: Donkey caravans link Mesopotamia and the Levant; Egypt's boats reach Byblos.
cent.-2800.art: Sumerian votive statues with wide eyes; Egyptian relief and the first stone architecture; megalithic tombs in Atlantic Europe.
cent.-2800.life: On the desert coast of Peru, in the Supe valley, Caral raises six platform mounds and two sunken round plazas; the largest mound stands 18 metres high, built of stones hauled up in reed bags. Its people make no pottery and have left no trace of war. They irrigate cotton for fishing nets and cloth, keep a knotted-string record, and play flutes of pelican bone. On the Pontic steppe, Yamnaya herders move with ox-drawn wagons and bury their chiefs, coated in ochre, under kurgans.
cent.-2800.food: Squash, beans, sweet potato, guava and lúcuma, roasted, with anchovies, sardines, clams and mussels at Caral, where plants made up more than 70 per cent of the diet; probably meat, milk products and mead on the steppe.
cent.-2800.smell: Caral smelled of food roasted over open fires, since there were no cooking pots, and of anchovies, sardines and shellfish carried up from the Pacific shore.
cent.-2800.trouble: Caral has no walls and no weapons, yet someone commands the labour that piles its mounds; on the steppe the kurgans, mostly for men, show where wealth and power are gathering.
cent.-2800.powers.2.t: the Kot Diji phase begins about 2800 BC
cent.-2700.moved: Stone, copper and timber move to Memphis for the first pyramids; Sumerian traders sail to Dilmun.
cent.-2700.art: The step pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, the first great stone building; Sumerian cylinder seals and inlaid lyres.
cent.-2700.life: Egypt becomes the Old Kingdom, a state of farmers. Most people live in mudbrick houses built to stay cool by day, each holding one family, and owe the king labour on canals and building sites. At Saqqara, Djoser’s step pyramid rises in stacked mastabas, the world’s first large-scale stone building and the first to stand taller than Jericho’s old tower. Children go naked until about twelve; a third die in infancy, and men who survive can expect to reach about thirty-five.
cent.-2700.food: Bread and beer, onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, dates and figs, with fish and fowl for all but the poorest, and wine and meat on feast days.
cent.-2700.smell: A Nile town smelled of bread baking in clay moulds set in the embers, of onions and garlic, and of the river mud the flood leaves behind.
cent.-2700.trouble: The question is the king’s claim on everyone’s time: farmers are taxed on the land they hold and called out in the corvée to cut canals and haul stone.
cent.-2700.powers.0.t: the Third Dynasty; Djoser's step pyramid
cent.-2700.powers.1.t: Gilgamesh of Uruk belongs to this age
cent.-2600.moved: Granite comes down the Nile from Aswan and limestone across it from Tura; lapis reaches Ur from Afghanistan; Indus seals are found in Mesopotamia.
cent.-2600.art: The Great Pyramid of Giza; the Standard of Ur and the gold of the royal tombs; the brick cities and bathing tank of Mohenjo-daro.
cent.-2600.life: On the Indus, cities are built to a plan. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro may each house 30,000 to 60,000 people in courtyard houses of baked brick on a grid, with some 700 wells at Mohenjo-daro, about one for every three houses, and covered drains under the main streets. Most townspeople are traders and craftsmen, shell-cutters and bead-makers, living street by street with their trade. No palace and no great temple has been found; the one public monument is a bath.
cent.-2600.food: Beef, buffalo, goat, pork and chicken with a little dairy, wheat, barley and pulses sown for the winter and rice, millets and beans for the summer.
cent.-2600.smell: A Harappan street smelled of wet brick and of bathwater running into the drains, and of shell and agate dust from the craftsmen’s quarters.
cent.-2600.trouble: The Indus cities leave no sign of kings, and almost every house has water and a drain, which suggests wealth spread unusually evenly; the question that will end them is water itself, as the region slowly dries.
cent.-2600.powers.0.t: the Fourth Dynasty; Khufu's pyramid finished about 2560 BC
cent.-2600.powers.2.t: the mature Harappan phase begins about 2600 BC
cent.-2500.moved: Copper from Oman and Cyprus, lapis from Badakhshan and Indus carnelian meet in the Gulf trade.
cent.-2500.art: The Sphinx and the pyramids of Giza; seated scribes in painted limestone; Indus steatite seals with unicorns; the first Stonehenge earthwork in Britain.
cent.-2500.life: At Giza a town grows beside the pyramids of Khafre and Menkaure, with communal sleeping halls, bakeries, breweries, kitchens, a copper workshop and a hospital. Ten thousand or more labourers, mostly from poor families, rotate through in three-month shifts; they are fed well, and buried with bread and beer in mudbrick tombs beside the king’s. In Sumer, at Ur, the royal dead go to the grave in gold and lapis with their lyres, and with between six and eighty attendants killed to follow them.
cent.-2500.food: Bread, beef and fish for the pyramid crews; barley bread and beer, dates, mutton and goat in Sumer.
cent.-2500.smell: The workers’ town at Giza smelled of bread ovens and breweries, of the copper workshop and of the cattle slaughtered to feed the crews.
cent.-2500.trouble: Who serves and who is served: Egypt’s pyramid crews are paid labourers, not slaves, but the death pits at Ur hold attendants killed, some by blows to the head, to go with their masters.
cent.-2500.powers.0.t: Khafre and Menkaure build at Giza
cent.-2500.powers.1.t: Lagash and Umma fight over water
cent.-2400.moved: Ebla's archive records textiles and metals moving across Syria; Egypt sends expeditions to Punt.
cent.-2400.art: The Pyramid Texts carved at Saqqara; the stele of the vultures at Lagash; the sarsen circle of Stonehenge about 2400 BC.
cent.-2400.life: In Syria, Ebla rules some 200,000 people, 40,000 of them in the capital, from a palace whose archive holds thousands of clay tablets. Its villages own the land and give the palace a yearly share; the kingdom counts about 140,000 sheep and goats and 9,000 cattle, and sends textiles and timber downriver to Kish. In Sumer, Urukagina of Lagash decrees that the rich must pay silver for what they buy from the poor and may not force a sale, and that widows and orphans go untaxed.
cent.-2400.food: Barley bread and beer, the measure of everything: Urukagina’s decree sets 80 loaves and 3 jugs of beer for a burial; at Ebla the palace feeds its permanent and seasonal workers from its own stores.
cent.-2400.smell: Ebla smelled of sheep and goats driven in from the pastures and of the wool and cloth that were its chief trade; a Sumerian town of bread ovens and beer.
cent.-2400.trouble: Debt and land: Urukagina’s reforms, the first known, limit what the rich may take from the poor, while Lagash and Umma fight on over irrigated fields and Ebla wars with Mari for the river trade.
cent.-2400.powers.0.t: the Fifth Dynasty and the sun temples
cent.-2400.powers.3.t: a Syrian kingdom with a great archive
cent.-2300.moved: Akkadian armies march to the Mediterranean and the Gulf; cedar from the Amanus and silver from Anatolia flow to Akkad.
cent.-2300.art: Naram-Sin's victory stele and the bronze head of an Akkadian king; the first cast-bronze statuary of Mesopotamia.
cent.-2300.life: Sargon of Akkad, a king with no royal father, makes himself master of Sumer and boasts that 5,400 men eat before him every day. His officials measure grain into the royal stores by a standard gur of about 300 litres; southern governors pay tax and send labourers, and most work in the great households is done by dependants paid in rations, slaves being few. His grandson Naram-Sin makes himself a god. On the lower Yangtze, the city of Liangzhu is abandoned to the floods.
cent.-2300.food: Barley, measured by the royal gur, as bread and beer, with dates and mutton; the great households pay their dependants in rations of grain.
cent.-2300.smell: An Akkadian city smelled of barley in the royal warehouses, of bread and beer made for the ration lines, and of the goods brought back from Dilmun and Magan.
cent.-2300.trouble: Empire itself is the quarrel: the old city-states rise against Akkad again and again, two of Sargon’s sons may have been murdered, and Naram-Sin calls himself King of the Four Quarters.
cent.-2300.powers.0.t: Sargon unites Sumer and Akkad from about 2334 BC
cent.-2300.powers.1.t: the long reign of Pepi II begins the decline
cent.-2200.moved: Drought and famine unsettle the Near East; the Gutians move into Mesopotamia from the Zagros.
cent.-2200.art: Gudea of Lagash's diorite statues; provincial Egyptian tomb painting; the last great Indus seal-cutting.
cent.-2200.life: A drought settles on the old world for most of a century. In northern Mesopotamia the plains empty around 2170 BC and perhaps 300,000 people flee south; the Gutians take Akkad, and a wall 180 kilometres long is raised against the Amorites. In Egypt low Nile floods coincide with the end of royal power: governors make their offices hereditary and raise their own armies, and the warlord Ankhtifi describes a land riven by hunger. In China the Longshan towns of Shandong decline.
cent.-2200.food: Less of everything: in Oman and the Gulf the winter winds salted the irrigated fields and cut the harvest to famine, and in Egypt every local lord claimed to have fed his own province while others went hungry.
cent.-2200.smell: The Near East smelled of dust: the dust laid down in the region records its driest years in centuries, from about 2310 to 2020 BC.
cent.-2200.trouble: Who keeps order when the state fails: Egypt splits between Heracleopolis and Thebes, Akkad falls, and the south walls itself off against the herders while refugees pour in.
cent.-2200.powers.1.n: Egypt in the First Intermediate Period
cent.-2100.moved: Ur's bureaucracy counts sheep and barley on tens of thousands of tablets; Amorites press in from the west.
cent.-2100.art: The ziggurat of Ur; Theban rock-cut tombs; the first Sumerian literary tablets.
cent.-2100.life: Ur rebuilds Sumer as a ledger. Under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi the scribes write some 120,000 surviving tablets; one office at Girsu manages 6,000 textile workers, mostly women and children, and the depot at Puzrish-Dagan moves 70,000 sheep in a year. Each province feeds the centre one month in twelve. Men and women in the state workshops are paid in barley and wool, sometimes oil, dates or beer. At Ur the ziggurat rises on a base 60 by 45 metres.
cent.-2100.food: Barley above all, paid out as wages with wool, oil, dates and beer, and sheep by the tens of thousands driven through the state depot.
cent.-2100.smell: Ur smelled of sheep pens and wool, of the looms of the state workshops and of barley being measured out by the royal gur.
cent.-2100.trouble: The state’s grip and its limits: the bala tax rotates through the provinces, Amorites appear in the records by the hundred, food runs short under Ibbi-Sin until Elam sacks Ur about 2004 BC, and in Egypt Mentuhotep II reunites the country by war about 2033 BC.
cent.-2000.moved: Assyrian merchants carry tin and textiles to Kanesh in Anatolia; the horse and the chariot spread from the steppe.
cent.-2000.art: Middle Kingdom portrait sculpture and the jewellery of Dahshur; the first Minoan palaces and Kamares ware; the Erlitou bronzes begin in China.
cent.-2000.life: Assur’s merchants run the first long-distance family firms. From the karum at Kanesh in central Anatolia they sell woollen cloth woven by their wives in Assur, send the silver home by caravan and write letters on clay; some 23,000 tablets survive from their houses. Women’s letters are warmer than the men’s, which are all business, and in Kanesh a woman named Zizizi lends money. In Egypt, reunited under the Middle Kingdom, bakers now raise bread in tall cones on square hearths.
cent.-2000.food: Barley bread and beer from Assur to Anatolia, with foodstuffs and spices among the caravan goods; in Egypt, emmer bread baked in cones, lentils, onions, fish and fowl.
cent.-2000.smell: The merchant quarter at Kanesh smelled of donkeys and their loads, of bales of wool and of the clay of letters being written and sealed.
cent.-2000.trouble: Trade and its rules: goods inside the karum go untaxed while they stay there, and families rather than the state carry the risk, while Egypt’s new kings rebuild the crown’s power after a century of division.
cent.-1900.moved: Donkey caravans run between Ashur and Kanesh; Nubian gold reaches Egypt through fortresses at the cataracts.
cent.-1900.art: Minoan fresco and faience; the Nubian forts of Buhen; the Story of Sinuhe copied in Egyptian schools.
cent.-1900.life: In the Luoyang basin Erlitou grows into a city of perhaps 24,000, with a palace quarter of twelve hectares inside rammed-earth walls and a bronze foundry run by its lords, the first in China to cast ritual vessels at scale; the ruts of its carts are the oldest in the country. On the Indus the great cities begin to empty from about 1900 BC as the land dries and people move east; the last skeletons show more violence and more disease.
cent.-1900.food: Millet in northern China, as porridge and even as noodles, like the millet noodles more than 4,000 years old found at Lajia in Qinghai; wheat, barley, rice and millets on the Indus.
cent.-1900.smell: Erlitou smelled of the foundry south of the palace, of copper brought from the Zhongtiao mountains being melted, and of rammed earth pounded for new walls.
cent.-1900.trouble: Who holds the sacred bronze: Erlitou’s elite keeps the casting of ritual vessels to itself, and whether its kings were the Xia of later legend is still argued; on the Indus the question is how to live when the rivers fail.
cent.-1900.powers.2.t: palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia
cent.-1800.moved: Hammurabi's armies take Larsa and Mari; letters move between Mari, Babylon and Aleppo by courier.
cent.-1800.art: The stele of Hammurabi; the painted palace of Mari; Minoan seal stones.
cent.-1800.life: Hammurabi of Babylon conquers his neighbours and, about 1753 BC, sets up a basalt stele 2.25 metres tall carved with laws that run to number 282. They sort people into the awilum, the lesser muskenum and the slave, and price every wrong: a surgeon earns ten shekels of silver for a successful operation with a bronze lancet and loses his hand if the patient dies; a builder whose house falls and kills its owner pays with his life. Boats, wagons, beasts and seasonal labourers all have fixed rates of hire.
cent.-1800.food: Barley bread and beer for most; written down about 1730 BC, the oldest recipes known: 25 stews, most of them of meat such as lamb, cooked with fat, leek, garlic, onion, cumin, coriander, beer, milk or blood.
cent.-1800.smell: A Babylonian kitchen smelled of garlic, leek and onion, of cumin and coriander, and of fat rendering in the stew pot.
cent.-1800.trouble: Justice by rank: an eye for an eye between equals, cheaper lives and smaller fines for the muskenum, and the slave as property, all set in stone by a conqueror who wants every subject to know the price.
cent.-1800.powers.0.t: the law code recorded about 1780 BC
cent.-1800.powers.2.t: the old palaces destroyed and rebuilt
cent.-1800.powers.3.t: a palace city on the Euphrates
cent.-1700.moved: The Hyksos bring the chariot to Egypt; the Indus cities are abandoned about 1700 BC.
cent.-1700.art: The new palace of Knossos with its bull-leaping frescoes; Erlitou bronze vessels; Babylonian terracotta plaques.
cent.-1700.life: On Crete the Minoan palaces are at their height. Knossos, with perhaps 20,000 to 100,000 people, is built round an open court, with red-painted wooden columns, light wells and great storerooms where the palace gathers the farms’ grain, oil and wine and gives them out again. Town houses rise two or three storeys, stone below and mud brick above, on paved and drained streets. Up the Nile, Kerma, Egypt’s rival in Nubia, has become a city of 25 hectares round the mudbrick temple of the Western Deffufa.
cent.-1700.food: Wheat, barley, chickpeas, grapes, figs and olive oil, the main cooking fat, with mutton, pork, goat and some fish on Crete; bread and the beef of great herds at Kerma.
cent.-1700.smell: A Minoan town smelled of olive oil and of wine made in the palace workshops, of sheep’s wool, the island’s cloth, and of the sea.
cent.-1700.trouble: Who gathers the surplus and who gives it out: the palaces of Crete and Nubia hold the stores, and the kings of Kerma, buried with thousands of cattle skulls and many sacrificed people, grow strong enough to challenge Egypt.
cent.-1600.moved: The Thera eruption darkens the Aegean; Mycenaean warriors rise on the mainland; bronze moves along the Yellow River.
cent.-1600.art: The frescoes of Akrotiri; the shaft graves of Mycenae and their gold masks; the ritual bronzes of early Shang.
cent.-1600.life: Around 1600 BC Thera blows apart in an eruption of the seventh magnitude, throwing out tens of cubic kilometres of rock; Akrotiri, warned by months of earthquakes, empties before the pumice buries it, and tsunamis strike the north coast of Crete. Egypt is divided: a dynasty of Levantine origin rules the Delta from Avaris, Thebes holds the south, and Kerma’s army raids deep into Upper Egypt. In China a later chronicle remembers yellow fog, a dim sun, frost in July and famine as the Xia gave way to the Shang.
cent.-1600.food: Bread, olive oil, figs and wine in the Aegean, from fields ploughed with donkeys and oxen; along the Nile, bakers of the new kingdom slap their dough onto the hot inner walls of cylindrical clay ovens.
cent.-1600.smell: Thera smelled of sulphur in the months of warning, before the ash and pumice came down over Akrotiri.
cent.-1600.trouble: Who will unite the Nile: Kamose and then Ahmose I of Thebes fight the kings of Avaris, intercept their letters to Kerma, and by about 1550 BC the Delta is Egyptian again.
cent.-1600.powers.0.t: the Shang dynasty begins about 1600 BC
cent.-1600.powers.1.t: the Hyksos expelled; the Eighteenth Dynasty
cent.-1600.powers.3.t: the eruption of Thera about 1600 BC buries Akrotiri
cent.-1500.moved: Egyptian armies and tribute move through Canaan; Mycenaeans take Knossos; the Punt expedition brings incense trees.
cent.-1500.art: Hatshepsut's terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari; the Theban tombs of the nobles; Mycenaean Linear B tablets.
cent.-1500.life: Egypt has annexed Nubia, and its kings are buried in the Valley of the Kings by a village of craftsmen. At Deir el-Medina some 68 mudbrick houses on stone footings, four or five rooms each, line one narrow street; the men work in two gangs, eight days on and two off, and the tomb scribe notes why they stay away: illness, a quarrel with a wife, a hangover. Many villagers, women too, can read. On Crete, about 1450 BC, Greek-speaking Mycenaean lords take over Knossos.
cent.-1500.food: Rations of grain, up to three times a field hand’s, made into bread by the wives and into beer brewed under the eye of the mistress of the house; an Egyptian labourer’s pay was about five and a half sacks of grain a month.
cent.-1500.smell: Deir el-Medina smelled of bread and brewing, of water carried up from a well half an hour’s walk away, and of stone dust from the royal tombs.
cent.-1500.trouble: Empire and its price: Egypt destroys Kerma and rules Nubia, the Nubians rebel for two centuries, and on Crete the palaces burn about 1470 BC before a Mycenaean elite takes Knossos.
cent.-1500.powers.0.t: Hatshepsut and Thutmose III; the empire reaches the Euphrates
cent.-1500.powers.1.t: walled capitals on the Yellow River
cent.-1500.powers.2.t: Hurrian kingdom of the upper Euphrates
cent.-1500.powers.3.t: warrior kings in Crete and the Argolid
cent.-1400.moved: Diplomatic letters in Akkadian pass between the great kings; the Uluburun ship carries copper, tin, glass and ebony.
cent.-1400.art: The Colossi of Memnon and the Luxor temple; the Amarna style under Akhenaten about 1350 BC; Shang oracle bones and the Fu Hao bronzes.
cent.-1400.life: The great kings of the Near East write to one another in Akkadian, and more than 300 of their clay letters turn up at Amarna, the city Akhenaten builds in haste about 1346 BC of whitewashed mud brick for his one god, the Aten, and which is abandoned soon after his death. In Greece the Mycenaean palaces of Pylos and Knossos keep Linear B accounts of land, rations and labour; the Knossos tablets count some 80,000 to 100,000 sheep, and women in palace workgroups weave the wool.
cent.-1400.food: Bread, beer, onions and fish along the Nile; in Greece, cereal given out by the palaces for festivals and communal meals, with olive oil, the chief export, and wine.
cent.-1400.smell: A Mycenaean palace smelled of perfumed oil, which its scribes watched as closely as bronze, and of the wool of its flocks; Akhetaten of fresh whitewash on mud brick.
cent.-1400.trouble: Faith and power: Akhenaten builds a city for one god, yet people there keep images of Bes, Taweret and Isis, and after him the court returns to Thebes and the old gods; in Greece the common people owe labour and taxes to the palace.
cent.-1400.powers.1.t: Suppiluliuma I makes Hatti a great power
cent.-1400.powers.2.t: the last Shang capital at Yin
cent.-1400.powers.3.t: palaces at Mycenae, Pylos and Thebes
cent.-1400.powers.4.t: Kassite kings as brother-monarchs of Egypt
cent.-1300.moved: Egyptian and Hittite armies meet on the Orontes; tin from Afghanistan and copper from Cyprus feed the bronze workshops.
cent.-1300.art: Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum; the Lion Gate of Mycenae; the Sanxingdui bronze masks of Sichuan.
cent.-1300.life: On the Huan river at Anyang the late Shang kings build a capital of some 25 square kilometres, a hundred times larger than any other site on the North China Plain, with rammed-earth halls and workshops for bronze and bone. Diviners crack turtle shells and ox shoulder blades and write question and answer on the bone: planting, wind and rain, war, childbirth. Commoners owe the king labour, not goods, and at least 14,197 human victims, half of them Qiang captives, are named in the inscriptions as sacrificed.
cent.-1300.food: Foxtail and broomcorn millet, the staple, and an ale of fermented millet poured from bronze jue for the great and from clay copies for the lesser; cattle, sheep, pigs and dogs went to the ancestors and then, probably, to the lords’ feasts.
cent.-1300.smell: Anyang smelled of its bronze and bone workshops, of the scorched shell and bone of the diviners, and of the blood of sacrifice.
cent.-1300.trouble: What the ancestors want: the kings ask them about every harvest and campaign and pay them in people and cattle, a thousand cattle in a single rite, while Fu Hao, queen and general, leads armies against the neighbours.
cent.-1300.powers.1.t: fights Egypt at Kadesh and makes the first known peace treaty
cent.-1300.powers.3.t: the Lion Gate and the tholos tombs
cent.-1200.moved: The Late Bronze Age collapse of about 1200–1150 BC: palaces burn from Pylos to Ugarit, the Sea Peoples move along the coasts and trade breaks down.
cent.-1200.art: Medinet Habu's reliefs of the sea battle; the last Mycenaean pottery; the Olmec begin at San Lorenzo in Mexico.
cent.-1200.life: Within a few decades after 1200 BC the palace world of the eastern Mediterranean breaks. Mycenae burns about 1190 BC and Pylos about 1180; Ugarit falls by 1178, its last king writing that enemy ships have come while his own are away. Ramesses III beats back the Sea Peoples but empties his treasury. At Deir el-Medina, in his 29th year, the royal tomb-builders, eighteen days into a month without rations, lay down their tools and sit in at the temples: the first strike on record.
cent.-1200.food: Grain was both wage and grievance: the strikers demanded grain, meat, oil and vegetables, and in one month received two bushels of emmer.
cent.-1200.smell: The Levantine coast smelled of burning cities, as Ugarit and Emar went up in flames between about 1187 and 1175 BC.
cent.-1200.trouble: Hunger, raiders and the failure of kings: drought in Anatolia, perhaps plague and the raids of the Sea Peoples strain every state at once, and in Greece writing itself is lost for four centuries.
cent.-1200.powers.0.t: Ramesses III fights the Sea Peoples
cent.-1100.moved: Iron begins to replace bronze; Phoenician ships work the Mediterranean; Aramaean and Israelite tribes settle the Levant.
cent.-1100.art: Olmec colossal heads at San Lorenzo; late Shang and early Zhou bronzes; Phoenician ivories.
cent.-1100.life: On the Gulf coast of Mexico the Olmec lords of San Lorenzo carve colossal heads, ten of them here, from basalt dragged from the Tuxtla mountains; moving one took perhaps 1,500 people three or four months. Most people live in villages on higher ground, each house with a lean-to and storage pits, planting the river banks between floods and clearing new fields with fire. They play a ballgame with balls of rubber. In China, about 1046 BC, the Zhou overthrow the last Shang king at Muye.
cent.-1100.food: Maize, beans, squash, cassava and sweet potato, with fish, turtles, deer and, at San Lorenzo, dog, the commonest meat of all; avocado and cacao probably grew beside the houses.
cent.-1100.smell: An Olmec village smelled of fields burned for planting, of river mud after the floods and of latex being worked into rubber.
cent.-1100.trouble: Who commands the water and the stone: an Olmec elite controls the rivers, the jade from Guatemala and the labour to move its monuments, though there is no sign of a standing army.
cent.-1100.powers.0.n: Egypt of the late New Kingdom
cent.-1100.powers.1.t: overthrown by the Zhou about 1046 BC
cent.-1000.moved: Phoenicians carry the alphabet and purple dye across the Mediterranean; iron weapons spread; horse nomads appear on the steppe.
cent.-1000.art: Zhou ritual bronzes with long inscriptions; Phoenician carved ivories; the geometric pottery of Athens.
cent.-1000.life: In the Wei valley the Zhou kings rule through kinsmen planted in colonies across the plain, and record each appointment and campaign in long inscriptions cast inside bronze vessels; human sacrifice, so common under the Shang, has stopped. On the Ganges plain the Vedic tribes are turning from cattle to the plough: iron axes and ploughs spread after 1000 BC, wheat, rice and barley go into big storage jars, and cattle are still the measure of wealth. Women milk, card wool, weave and grind the grain.
cent.-1000.food: Milk and dairy, grains, fruit and vegetables on the Ganges, with meat but not the cow, and the drinks soma and sura; millet, meat and ale at the Zhou ancestral feasts.
cent.-1000.smell: A Vedic village smelled of cattle and milk, of the dyer’s vats and of grain stored in jars; a Zhou hall of millet ale and meat at the feasts for the ancestors.
cent.-1000.trouble: Who may rule: the Zhou claim the favour of Tian, heaven, for their conquest, while in India the rajan answers to the councils of the sabha and samiti and a hierarchy of varna begins to set.
cent.-1000.powers.0.t: the Zhou rule from the Wei valley
cent.-1000.powers.1.n: Egypt of the Third Intermediate Period
cent.-1000.powers.2.t: a lull before the Neo-Assyrian empire
cent.-1000.powers.3.t: the alphabet spreads with the traders
cent.-1000.powers.4.t: the age of David and Solomon in tradition
cent.-900.moved: Assyrian armies march yearly for tribute; Phoenicians found Carthage in 814 BC; Greeks begin to sail west.
cent.-900.art: Assyrian palace reliefs at Nimrud; the geometric style of Greece; Olmec jade.
cent.-900.life: Assyria makes war a yearly business. Ashurnasirpal II builds Kalhu, at Nimrud, as his new capital: walls 7.5 kilometres long round 360 hectares, a palace guarded by winged, man-headed lions, and gardens and a zoo stocked from his campaigns. Governors, deputies and village managers collect the taxes in labour and in goods. In Greece, emerging from its dark age, only four places hold more than a thousand people, and by 900 BC almost every weapon laid in a grave is of iron.
cent.-900.food: For the ten-day feast that opened Kalhu in 864 BC, 69,574 guests, 16,000 of them townspeople, got through 10,000 pigeons, 10,000 jugs of beer and 10,000 skins of wine, among countless other things.
cent.-900.smell: Kalhu smelled of new mud brick, of beer and wine for the king’s feasts, and of the botanical garden and zoo filled with the plants and beasts of conquered lands.
cent.-900.trouble: Tribute or ruin: the Assyrian army marches out to collect, with cavalry and siege engines for those who refuse, and by the next century whole peoples are deported by the tens of thousands.
cent.-900.powers.0.t: Ashurnasirpal II builds a new capital
cent.-900.powers.3.t: colonies founded westward; Carthage in 814 BC
cent.-900.powers.4.t: Nubian power at the fourth cataract
cent.-800.moved: Greeks adopt the Phoenician alphabet and plant colonies in Sicily and Italy; Rome is founded by tradition in 753 BC; the Homeric poems take shape.
cent.-800.art: Greek geometric vases; Assyrian reliefs of lion hunts; the Etruscans begin at Tarquinia and Veii.
cent.-800.life: Greece comes out of its dark age with the Phoenician alphabet, to which it adds vowels, and with more people: the population roughly doubles in the eighth century and villages merge into cities, Athens growing from perhaps 1,500 people towards 5,000. In Sicily and southern Italy a new Greek town is founded about every other year, and the first Olympic games are held in 776 BC. Houses average 45 to 50 square metres, and barely half of children live to eighteen.
cent.-800.food: Barley or the preferred wheat, pulses, fruit and vegetables from small, mixed farms, olives and grapes for oil and wine to sell, and sheep and goats for milk, wool and meat.
cent.-800.smell: A Greek village smelled of olive oil and new wine, of sheep and goats folded near the houses, and of their dung carried out to the fields.
cent.-800.trouble: Land and debt, as people multiply and the work falls to slaves, sharecroppers and debtors; in China the Zhou capital is sacked in 771 BC and the court flees east, and on the Nile Piye of Kush takes Lower Egypt about 727 BC.
cent.-800.powers.0.t: the dominant power of the Near East
cent.-800.powers.1.t: falls in 771 BC; the court moves to Luoyang
cent.-800.powers.2.t: the first Olympic Games in 776 BC
cent.-800.powers.3.t: Tyre's colony on the African coast
cent.-800.powers.4.t: Assyria's rival in the Armenian highlands
cent.-700.moved: Assyrian deportations move whole peoples; Greek colonists settle the Black Sea and Sicily; Scythians ride into the Near East.
cent.-700.art: The library and reliefs of Nineveh under Ashurbanipal; Corinthian orientalising pottery; Etruscan tomb painting.
cent.-700.life: Assyria rules by tax, corvée and deportation. Sennacherib rebuilds Nineveh with a wall 12 kilometres long and 25 metres high and a park that may lie behind the legend of the Hanging Gardens; his successors take Memphis in 671 BC and sack Thebes in 663, driving the Kushite pharaohs back to Napata. Aramaic, carried by the deported, becomes the common tongue of the region. In Lydia, about 650 BC, the first coins are struck, and in Greece armoured hoplites fight in close ranks.
cent.-700.food: Bread, beer and wine in Assyria, where village managers take part of every harvest as tax; wheat or barley, pulses, olive oil and wine in Greece.
cent.-700.smell: Nineveh smelled of new brick and the king’s great park; far up the Nile, Meroë smelled of iron bloomeries, whose fuel stripped the Butana plain of its forests and left heaps of slag.
cent.-700.trouble: Empire and resistance: Judah, aided by Kush, defies Sennacherib in 701 BC, and in 612 the Medes and Babylonians take Nineveh after a two-month siege and loot it; in Greek cities tyrants such as Cypselus of Corinth take power from the nobles.
cent.-700.powers.0.t: Sennacherib's capital; Egypt conquered in 671 BC
cent.-700.powers.2.t: Sparta, Corinth and Athens; Greek colonies from Marseille to the Black Sea
cent.-600.moved: Judaeans are carried to Babylon; Greek philosophy begins at Miletus; coinage spreads from Lydia; the Buddha and Confucius are born within a generation.
cent.-600.art: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon; the first marble kouroi of Greece and the temple of Artemis at Ephesus about 550 BC; Persepolis is not yet begun.
cent.-600.life: On the Ganges plain India builds its first great cities since the Indus: sixteen kingdoms and republics from Gandhara to Anga, with Kashi at Varanasi, Kausambi a trading town and Magadha rising. Wandering teachers challenge the Vedic priests, and Buddhism and Jainism are born. In Athens, Solon, made mediator in 594 BC, ends slavery for debt and makes income, not birth, the test for office. Cyrus founds the Persian empire; by 500 BC it may hold 17 to 35 million people.
cent.-600.food: Rice, wheat, barley and milk on the Ganges plain; barley or wheat, olive oil, pulses and wine in Greece; and in Persia grain as tribute, 120,000 measures a year from Egypt alone.
cent.-600.smell: An Indian market town smelled of cattle and milk, of leather and dye, and of the potter’s kiln.
cent.-600.trouble: Debt and who counts as a citizen: Athens’ poor work off their debts as bondsmen until Solon ends it, India’s new kingdoms swallow its republics, and Persia makes the whole Near East one tribute-paying state.
cent.-600.powers.0.t: Nebuchadnezzar II, reigning 605–562 BC, after the fall of Nineveh in 612
cent.-600.powers.2.t: Egypt revived under the Twenty-sixth Dynasty
cent.-600.powers.3.t: the hegemon states; Confucius born 551 BC
cent.-600.powers.4.t: Solon's laws; lyric poets on Lesbos
cent.-600.powers.5.t: the Buddha and Mahavira teach here
cent.-500.moved: The Royal Road carries Persian couriers from Susa to Sardis; Persian armies cross to Greece; iron and coinage spread through India and China.
cent.-500.art: The Apadana reliefs of Persepolis; red-figure vases of Athens; the archaic smile gives way to the severe style; the first Buddhist communities.
cent.-500.life: Athens at its height may hold 250,000 to 300,000 people. When the Spartans invade in 431 BC, the farmers of Attica crowd inside the Long Walls, tripling the numbers there, and in 430 a plague kills 75,000 to 100,000, about a quarter of the people; the sick die alone and the temples fill with corpses. In Persia, Darius’s scribes at Persepolis write more than 10,000 tablets on the empire’s stores, and couriers ride the 2,500-kilometre Royal Road in fifteen days.
cent.-500.food: Wheat or barley, olive oil, pulses and wine in Greece; in Persia, tribute in kind fed court and army, Babylon alone sending four months’ food for the army each year.
cent.-500.smell: Athens in the plague years smelled of the dead, heaped together in the streets and temples or thrown onto pyres already burning.
cent.-500.trouble: Who leads the Greeks: Athens and Sparta go to war in 431 BC, and inside the walls the plague breaks law and piety, as the rich die and their wealth passes to poorer kin.
cent.-500.powers.0.t: Darius I rules from the Indus to Thrace
cent.-500.powers.1.t: the young democracy; Marathon in 490 BC
cent.-500.powers.4.t: the Warring States begin; Confucius dies 479 BC
cent.-500.powers.5.t: the rising kingdom of the Ganges
cent.-400.moved: Xenophon's ten thousand march home through Persia; Celts move into Italy and the Danube lands; crossbows and iron ploughs spread in China.
cent.-400.art: The Parthenon finished in 432 BC and the statue of Zeus at Olympia in 435; Praxiteles at Athens; the lacquers and bells of Zeng in China.
cent.-400.life: In China the state of Qin remakes its people for farming and war. From 356 BC Shang Yang’s laws punish anyone who knows of a crime and fails to report it as harshly as the criminal, reward farmers who beat their harvest quotas, tax twice the households that keep several grown sons under one roof, and rank soldiers in twenty grades by what they achieve in battle. Alexander marches from Macedon in 334 BC with about 48,000 men, founds more than twenty cities and dies at Babylon in 323.
cent.-400.food: Wheat or barley, olive oil, pulses and wine in the Greek world that Alexander carries east; on Qin’s farms the harvest itself was the test, rewarded above the quota and punished below it.
cent.-400.smell: An army on Alexander’s road smelled of some 48,000 men and 6,100 horses, a moving city that marched for ten years from Macedon to the Indus and back to Babylon.
cent.-400.trouble: How to rule many peoples: Alexander marries his officers to Persian noblewomen at Susa and gives Persians commands, to his own soldiers’ anger, while in India the Nanda kings of Magadha swallow the old kingdoms from about 345 BC and in Qin the law reaches into every household.
cent.-400.powers.1.t: Sparta victorious in 404 BC; Socrates executed 399 BC
cent.-400.powers.2.t: takes Veii; sacked by Gauls about 390 BC
cent.-400.powers.3.t: at war with Syracuse for Sicily
cent.-400.powers.4.t: seven great states; Mozi and Mencius
cent.-300.moved: Greek settlers and language spread from Egypt to Bactria; Ashoka's missions carry Buddhism to Sri Lanka; elephants and grain move in Hellenistic armies.
cent.-300.art: Hellenistic Alexandria, Pergamon and Rhodes: the Colossus of about 280 BC, the Nike of Samothrace later; Ashoka's pillars; the great wall sections of the Chinese states.
cent.-300.life: India is one empire for the first time. From Pataliputra, behind a wooden wall with 64 gates and 570 towers, the Mauryas count their subjects by trade and claim all the land, giving seed, tools and grain reserves in return for tribute. After the Kalinga war of 261 BC kills some 100,000 people, Ashoka turns to the Buddha’s teaching and has wells dug, trees planted along the roads and medicine given to people and animals. In Kush the kings now go to their pyramids at Meroë.
cent.-300.food: The grain of the fertile eastern Ganges plain, held in royal reserves against hard years, and under Ashoka an edict against killing wild animals.
cent.-300.smell: Pataliputra smelled of wood smoke and timber, a city walled in wood, and of the cargoes of the river trade; Meroë smelled of its iron furnaces.
cent.-300.trouble: War and conscience: after Kalinga, Ashoka’s edicts preach restraint across India while thirty commissioners in the capital regulate wages, trade and sales taxes, and occupations harden into castes.
cent.-300.powers.0.t: Alexander's heirs from Syria to Bactria
cent.-300.powers.1.t: the Museum and Library; the lighthouse about 280 BC
cent.-300.powers.3.t: master of central Italy after the Samnite wars
cent.-200.moved: Roman legions cross to Greece; the Xiongnu confederation presses the Han; the Silk Road begins to carry Chinese silk westward.
cent.-200.art: Pergamene baroque and the altar of Pergamon; the terracotta army at Mount Li; Han lacquer and silk; the stupa of Sanchi.
cent.-200.life: The Han rule China for four centuries. Small landowning farmers rank just below scholars and officials; tenants, labourers and slaves come lower, and registered merchants must wear white and pay heavy taxes. Families of four or five live together, and men are called up at 23 for a year’s training and a year’s service. Zhang Qian’s journeys west, 139 to 125 BC, open the road that becomes the Silk Road. In Rome, Tiberius Gracchus is killed in 133 BC for giving public land to the poor.
cent.-200.food: Wheat, barley, millet, rice and beans, with pork, poultry, mutton, fish and game, seasoned with soy sauce, salt, honey and sugar, washed down with beer and yellow wine; from the west came sesame, peas, onions, coriander and cucumber.
cent.-200.smell: A Han county town smelled of the state’s iron works and salt, of pigs, ducks and geese, and of beer and yellow wine.
cent.-200.trouble: Who owns the land and who works it: in Italy great estates worked by slaves push the Gracchi to land reform and Sicily’s slaves to revolt in 138 BC, while in China the state takes salt and iron into its own hands in 117 BC.
cent.-200.powers.1.t: Hannibal beaten at Zama in 202 BC
cent.-200.powers.2.t: Antiochus III; soon humbled by Rome
cent.-100.moved: Silk reaches Rome and Roman glass reaches China by way of Parthia; Mithridates fights Rome in Asia; the monsoon route to India opens.
cent.-100.art: Late Republican portrait busts; the Gandharan Buddha is about to appear; Han tomb figures and bronze mirrors.
cent.-100.life: Rome rules the Mediterranean and cannot govern itself. The Social War of 91 to 87 BC triples the number of citizens; Sulla’s soldiers kill for profit and his lists make murder legal. In 73 BC some seventy gladiators break out of a school near Capua, and Spartacus leads an army of about 70,000; when Crassus wins, 6,000 are crucified along the Appian Way. From 58 BC the citizens of Rome get their grain free. In Mexico the first buildings of Teotihuacan rise; in Nubia, Kandake Amanirenas fights Roman Egypt.
cent.-100.food: Free grain for the citizens of Rome from 58 BC, made into bread and porridge, with olive oil, wine and garum, the fermented fish sauce traded across the sea.
cent.-100.smell: In 71 BC the Appian Way smelled of death for more than a hundred miles, where 6,000 of Spartacus’ followers hung on crosses between Capua and Rome.
cent.-100.trouble: Land, citizenship and the army: the Italian allies fight Rome for the vote, generals turn their legions on the city, and Caesar crosses the Rubicon in 49 BC and is killed in 44.
cent.-100.powers.0.t: Marius and Sulla; the provinces of Asia and Africa
cent.-100.powers.1.t: Emperor Wu's expansion to Central Asia
cent.-100.powers.2.t: heirs of the Seleucids in Iran and Iraq
cent.0.moved: Monsoon ships sail from Egypt to India; Jesus is born in Judaea; the legions are lost in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9.
cent.0.art: The Ara Pacis and the Augustus of Prima Porta; the wall paintings of Pompeii; the Pyramid of the Sun begun at Teotihuacan.
cent.0.life: Under Augustus the Roman Empire holds some 55 to 60 million people, a sixth to a quarter of the world. In Italy one person in four or five is a slave; the top one and a half per cent of households take a fifth of all income, and the great majority live near subsistence. Inscriptions in Rome name 268 trades, and enslaved men and women in the city die, on average, at about seventeen. In Mexico the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan nears completion, 65 metres high.
cent.0.food: Bread from shipped grain, the empire’s chief cargo, with olive oil, wine and garum, the fermented fish sauce sold in jars across the empire.
cent.0.smell: A Roman town smelled of garum and olive oil in the shops, of wine, and of the crowds and furnaces of the public baths.
cent.0.trouble: Who shares the peace: a near-subsistence majority under a tiny rich elite, slaves freed so often that a law of 2 BC limits how many an owner may free in his will, and freedmen rising so high in the emperor’s service that Hadrian will curb them.
cent.0.powers.3.t: steppe peoples in Bactria and the Punjab
cent.0.powers.5.t: the great city of Mexico rising
cent.100.moved: Buddhism travels the Silk Road into China; Roman coins pile up in south India; Christian communities spread round the eastern Mediterranean.
cent.100.art: Trajan's Column and Forum; the Pantheon rebuilt 118–128; the Gandharan Buddha in Greek drapery; the Mathura school.
cent.100.life: At Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico the Pyramid of the Sun is finished by about AD 100, and the city fills with some 2,000 walled apartment compounds of 60 to 100 people each, with whole neighbourhoods of migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf coast and obsidian workshops that make the city rich. In the Roman Empire a plague that seems to start at the siege of Seleucia in 165 kills perhaps 5 to 10 million, about one in ten; Marcus Aurelius fills the ranks with gladiators, slaves and bandits.
cent.100.food: Maize, beans, amaranth, tomatillos and pumpkins at Teotihuacan; in Han China, wheat, barley, millet, rice and beans, with pork and poultry, soy sauce and yellow wine.
cent.100.smell: Teotihuacan smelled of cooking fires in thousands of apartment courtyards and of the textiles and pottery made in its neighbourhood workshops.
cent.100.trouble: In China the Yellow Turbans rise across eight provinces in 184 and are crushed within a year; in Rome the plague empties the legions just as Germanic invaders break in, driven out only by 171.
cent.100.powers.0.t: Trajan; the empire at its greatest extent by 117
cent.100.powers.1.t: the Eastern Han; paper in use
cent.100.powers.2.t: Kanishka's realm from Bactria to the Ganges
cent.100.powers.4.t: the largest city of the Americas
cent.200.moved: Plague and soldier-emperors unsettle Rome; Goths reach the Black Sea; the Sasanians revive Persia.
cent.200.art: The Severan arch and the baths of Caracalla; the Buddhist caves of Ajanta begin; Maya stelae at Tikal.
cent.200.life: The Roman world nearly breaks. Between 235 and 284 at least 26 men claim the throne, the silver coinage is debased with bronze and copper until prices run away, and some taxes are taken in kind. A plague from about 251 to 262 is said to cut the people of Alexandria by 62 per cent. Cities shrink and build thick walls, Rome among them; townspeople move out to the land, and small farmers bind themselves to great estates as coloni. In China the Han fall in 220.
cent.200.food: Bread, oil and wine, more and more from the estate one lived on, as trade broke down and landowners turned to subsistence farming and barter.
cent.200.smell: A Roman town smelled of lime and mortar from the thick new walls going up round its shrinking streets.
cent.200.trouble: Who can hold the empire together: Gaul and Britain break away under their own emperors from 260, Zenobia of Palmyra takes Syria and Egypt, and Aurelian wins them back by 274.
cent.200.powers.1.t: the Han fall in 220; the Three Kingdoms
cent.300.moved: Armenia adopts Christianity in 301 and Rome tolerates it in 313; Constantinople is founded in 330; nomads pour into north China.
cent.300.art: The Arch of Constantine; early Christian catacomb painting and the first basilicas; Gupta sculpture begins; the Maya carve their stelae.
cent.300.life: The Roman Empire survives by taxing harder. Diocletian’s army is said to have counted 389,704 men and his fleets 45,562; gold buys two and a half times as much as it did in 274, a sign of a gold-rich elite over a cash-poor peasantry. In Armorica almost every villa is deserted by 350, and money stops changing hands there about 360. In 376 Goths fleeing the Huns cross the Danube, and in 378 they destroy an eastern army at Adrianople. In India the Guptas rise from about 320.
cent.300.food: In the Roman West, what the farm grew rather than what the market sold, as the villas emptied and coin went out of use; in India, pepper among the luxuries shipped west with silk, ivory and pearls.
cent.300.smell: A fort on the Rhine smelled of the plough and the byre, its soldiers now paid in land rather than wages.
cent.300.trouble: Who carries the cost of defence: heavy taxes ruin trades and city councils lose their revenues, and by 400 Armorica is held not by the emperor but by the bagaudae.
cent.300.powers.2.t: China briefly reunited, then overrun from the north
cent.400.moved: Goths, Vandals and Huns move across the empire; Patrick goes to Ireland in 432; pilgrims like Faxian travel from China to India.
cent.400.art: The mosaics of Ravenna begin; the Ajanta paintings; the Yungang Buddhas of the Northern Wei; Gupta temples at Sanchi.
cent.400.life: The Western Empire comes apart. In 405 and 406 perhaps 100,000 Germanic and Alan people cross the Rhine; Alaric’s siege starves Rome, which in 410 is sacked for three days, the first time an enemy has taken it in eight centuries, and in 476 Odoacer sends the imperial regalia to Constantinople. In Gupta India the Chinese monk Faxian, travelling between 405 and 411, finds offences punished by fines rather than death and no register of households. Teotihuacan holds perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 people.
cent.400.food: In Gupta India, Faxian found, people killed no living creature, drank no intoxicants and ate no onions or garlic; in southern China tea was now drunk; in Rome, under siege from 408 to 410, there was famine.
cent.400.smell: A late Roman town smelled more of the farmyard and less of the bath-house, as its council lost its revenues and let its public services lapse.
cent.400.trouble: Who protects the provinces: the Western army dwindles until Stilicho drafts 12,000 prisoners, frontier land is given up to the Germans, and from the late fifth century the Huns break into India.
cent.400.powers.0.t: divided after Theodosius; Rome sacked in 410
cent.500.moved: Belisarius retakes Africa and Italy from 533; plague from Egypt reaches Constantinople in 541–542; Buddhism reaches Japan from Baekje in 538 or 552.
cent.500.art: Hagia Sophia and the mosaics of San Vitale; the Longmen caves; the first Buddhist images of Japan.
cent.500.life: In 541 plague comes to Constantinople on the grain ships from Egypt and may kill 40 per cent of the city, up to 5,000 a day at its height by modern estimates. Tax revenues fall as farms empty, landowners are made to pay the tax on their dead neighbours’ fields, and in Egypt wages rise by up to 150 per cent. In Mexico, about 550, Teotihuacan’s palaces are sacked and burned after drought; in India the last Gupta kings give way to the Huns.
cent.500.food: Egyptian grain, the bread of Constantinople, carried in the same ships that carried the plague; in southern China, tea, drunk there since the fifth century.
cent.500.smell: Constantinople in 542 smelled of the unburied dead, stacked in the open because there was no room left to bury them.
cent.500.trouble: Who pays when people die: the Eastern Empire squeezes the survivors for the taxes of the dead, while the burning of Teotihuacan, aimed mostly at the rulers’ buildings, may have been a revolt from within.
cent.600.moved: The Grand Canal joins the Yangtze and Yellow rivers; Arab armies take Syria, Persia and Egypt within two decades of 632; Xuanzang walks to India.
cent.600.art: Tang Chang'an, the largest city on earth; Horyu-ji in Nara; Sutton Hoo in England; Visigothic votive crowns.
cent.600.life: In 609 a census counts about 50 million people in China, and from 618 the Tang rule them from Chang’an, a walled grid more than ten kilometres across, cut into 108 walled wards with four gates each and two supervised markets. Each family is allotted a nominal 100 mu of land and owes grain, cloth and labour. In Arabia, a man of the Quraysh of Mecca, Muhammad, begins to preach about 613, leaves for Medina in 622 and, with 10,000 followers, takes Mecca in 630.
cent.600.food: Barley, garlic, turnips, soybeans, pears, peaches, jujubes and pomegranates in Tang China, with pork, chicken and, in the north, lamb; in Arabia, the dates of oases such as Khaybar and Fadak.
cent.600.smell: Chang’an smelled of the goods of its two great markets and of the dust of its avenues; Mecca, of camels and the caravans loading for Syria.
cent.600.trouble: Faith and clan: the Quraysh boycott Muhammad’s clan from about 616 to 619, the Constitution of Medina binds Arab and Jewish tribes to defend the oasis together, and in China the rich begin to buy up the land the equal-field system was meant to share.
cent.600.powers.1.t: Khosrow II takes Jerusalem and Egypt
cent.600.powers.2.t: the Sui reunited China in 581; the Tang from 618
cent.600.powers.4.t: the last great north Indian empire before the Muslims
cent.600.powers.5.t: the Hijra in 622; the conquests from 632
cent.700.moved: Paper-making passes west after Talas in 751; Arab dirhams reach Scandinavia; Vikings strike Lindisfarne in 793.
cent.700.art: The Dome of the Rock and the Umayyad mosque of Damascus; the Great Mosque of Córdoba from 785; Tang three-colour glaze; Nara's bronze Buddha; the Lindisfarne Gospels.
cent.700.life: In 762 the Abbasids found Baghdad, a round walled city with four gates, built by a workforce of 100,000; by 794 it has a paper mill, and soon it is known for its bookshops. Christians and Jews keep their faith and pay the jizya, and an elite household may own a thousand slaves. In China the An Lushan rebellion of 755 to 763 ends the Tang golden age, and in 780 the old taxes in grain, cloth and labour give way to a cash tax paid twice a year.
cent.700.food: In Chang’an, for those who could pay, golden peaches from Samarkand, pistachios and figs from Persia and mangoes from the south, and sugar from cane, learned from India in the seventh century; from Baghdad’s world, sugar, almonds and citrus travel west to Spain.
cent.700.smell: Baghdad smelled of its new trades: sugar boiling, rope and matting, silk and textiles, and the paper mill of 794.
cent.700.trouble: Who belongs: non-Arab Muslims push into the elite and non-Muslims pay their tax as protected subjects, while in China the rebellion breaks the dynasty’s hold on its own provinces.
cent.700.powers.0.t: from Spain (711) to Sind; the Dome of the Rock 692
cent.700.powers.1.t: Empress Wu; Li Bai and Du Fu to come
cent.800.moved: Vikings sail to Seville and Paris and settle Iceland about 870; Rurik rules at Novgorod from 862; Greek science is translated at Baghdad.
cent.800.art: Borobudur; the Palatine chapel at Aachen; Abbasid Samarra; the Book of Kells; Tang poetry at its height.
cent.800.life: Since the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, the Northmen are at sea. At home they live on farms of free karls under the jarls, with thralls, as much as a quarter of the people, doing the hardest work; captives are sold east for Arab silver, and Iceland is settled. In the Maya lowlands Tikal, Copán and Calakmul fall silent: dated monuments drop from about forty a year around 750 to none by 900, as the rains fail by up to half. In Iraq the enslaved Zanj rise in 869.
cent.800.food: Porridge and bread of barley and wheat, meat cured, smoked or made into sausages, cod, salmon, herring and seal, skyr, butter and cheese, beer and mead; the poor man’s bread was gritty from the quern and full of weed seeds.
cent.800.smell: A Norse farm smelled of meat curing in the smoke, of herring and seal, of butter and skyr, and of beer and mead.
cent.800.trouble: Raid, trade and slavery: weapon injuries scar 72 per cent of the examined men of Viking Age Norway and 42 per cent of the women, slaves go east for silver, and in the Maya south the divine kings lose their hold as the rain fails.
cent.800.powers.0.t: Charlemagne crowned at Rome on 25 December 800
cent.800.powers.1.t: Harun al-Rashid; the House of Wisdom
cent.800.powers.2.t: recovering from the An Lushan rebellion
cent.900.moved: Varangians row to Constantinople; Otto I is crowned in 962; Vladimir has Kiev baptised in 988; the Norse reach Greenland in 985.
cent.900.art: The mosques and libraries of Córdoba; Byzantine ivories and enamels; Ferdowsi writing the Shahnameh; the Song begin painted landscape.
cent.900.life: The Rus’ princes of Kiev ride out each year on the poliudie to gather tribute in money, furs or slaves, and send furs, beeswax, honey and slaves down the Dnieper on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks. Most of their five million or so subjects grow grain and keep livestock. In 988 Vladimir orders Kiev baptised. In the Yucatán the northern cities of Chichén Itzá and Uxmal carry on after the south has emptied, and the Copán valley holds 15,000 people, about half its peak.
cent.900.food: Cereal porridge and bread with the meat and milk of their beasts, and honey, which the Rus’ also sold south to Constantinople.
